The B.S. program in interdisciplinary neuroscience will provide students with foundational knowledge of the nervous system including a broad array of areas such as development of the nervous system, brain structure and function, cellular and molecular biology, neuropharmacology, neuroethics, research methods, as well as knowledge of neurodegenerative disease and psychological/psychiatric disorders.
The undergraduate program offers three major options (tracks): a B.S. degree with a major in Clinical Neuroscience from the College of Health Sciences, a B.S. degree with a major in Molecular Neuroscience from the College of Environment and Life Sciences, and a B.S. degree with a major in Neuropharmacology from the College of Pharmacy.
The option for choosing between three different neuroscience majors is a unique andstrength makesto thisthe URI majorneuroscience trulyeducational distinct with regard to undergraduate educationexperience.
Please note: students may only earn a Neuroscience degree in one track due to the overlapping of preparation and core courses needed for the major.

Careers Students who graduate with thisa B.S. in interdisciplinary neuroscience have an ever-growing choice of career options.
These include graduate school in neuroscience, medical school, graduate programs in medical and allied health professions; research positions in academic, government, biotech or pharmaceutical laboratories; and a variety of professional opportunities in science education, science writing, data science, and health care.

Program will be flexible to include in person and online courses on the regular academic calendar, prior assessment of learning, transfer credits, and credit for internship and/or co-op work experience.
The program is underpinned by career readiness competencies and the principles of responsible management education (PRME), which are focused on sustainable development.
It promotes hands-on learning and prepares students for rewarding career opportunities through an intentional curriculum which includes up to 12 credits for internships, co-ops, or work experience. it will help prepare students to lead change and to make a societal impact.
Students will learn about stakeholder inclusion, emotional intelligence, and how to facilitate creativity.
The flexible curriculum will allow them to engage with courses in other disciplines to prepare them to focus on topics like equitable growth, responsible use of natural resources, and management of human- technology interactions, including challenges associated with reskilling workers in light of emerging technologies.

This will allow them to position themselves for opportunities in a market that values strong organizational performance, continuous innovation, and sustainability and trust.
The program overlaps with the Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, which is offered by the same College.
The BA has a more interdisciplinary focus, encourages more engagement with other disciplines, and offers more flexibility to take electives and minors that can lead to specialization toward specific career paths (e.g. sales, digital retailing, sports management, non-profit management, sustainability management, etc.).
In contrast, the existing, AACSB-accredited BSBA majors fix 76 - 81 of 120 credits for BSBA students and cap internship credits at 6 elective credits.

As the landscape of education continues to evolve, there is a growing need for skilled leaders who can navigate the complexities of educational institutions, implement effective policies, and drive meaningful change.
Effective principals have substantial positive impacts on student achievement.
Research demonstrates that replacing a below-average principal with an above-average one can significantly increase student learning in both math and reading annually.
Beyond student achievement, principals also affect other crucial outcomes such as student attendance, discipline, and teacher retention.
Effective principals are linked to reduced absenteeism and exclusionary discipline, as well as higher teacher job satisfaction and lower turnover rates, particularly among high-performing teachers.
Principals who engage in instructionally focused interactions with teachers, such as providing feedback, coaching, and developing a data-driven instructional program, contribute to positive school outcomes.
These practices emphasize the importance of principals being deeply involved in the instructional aspects of their schools.
Principals play a crucial role in addressing educational equity.

Effective leaders are adept at creating inclusive environments that support diverse student populations.
This involves strategic hiring, fostering collaborative cultures, and ensuring equitable allocation of resources.
Rhode Island, like many other states, is facing a shortage of school administrators.
According to data collected by the Rhode Island Department of Education for the 2021-22 school year, 46 administrator vacancies were reported by 41 Local Education Agencies (LEAs), representing 8% of building-level administrator positions statewide.
Nationally, the National Center for Education Statistics (2023) found that about one in ten public school principals left the profession between the 2020-21 and 2021-22 school years.
This highlights the urgent need for strong principal preparation programs that equip future leaders with the skills required for effective school leadership.
Ongoing professional development and support are critical to ensure principals have the tools necessary to succeed (Grissom, Egalite, and Lindsay, 2021).
